description:
We are a team of three third-year Italian high school students passionate about science, technology, and programming.

For this project, one member focused on researching Mars' environmental conditions, physical constraints, and real-world challenges to ensure scientific realism. The other two led the game design, development, and programming, transforming these scientific concepts into an engaging and realistic simulation.
summary:
​Make Mars Great Again is an immersive survival and management simulation designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Tailored specifically for young explorers aged 7 to 12, the game transforms complex aerospace engineering into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. Players step into the boots of a Martian astronaut, tasked with building a sustainable base by managing vital resources like oxygen, water, energy, and food.
​By blending authentic space concepts (such as ISRU resource extraction and historical space weather patterns from NASA’s DONKI database) with an intuitive achievement-guided progression and educational machinery logs, the project bridges the gap between gaming and STEM education, empowering the next generation of space pioneers
details:
Make Mars Great Again is a 2D pixel-art Martian outpost simulation and survival strategy game created for Challenge 3 of the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Designed for young learners aged 7 to 12, the game puts players in charge of an astronaut who must establish a sustainable human outpost on Mars.

How the game works

Players land with a mission budget, limited rations, and a finite supply of suit oxygen. They explore on foot or in a rover that can recharge using its own solar panels. They collect geological samples, deploy research drills, and use laboratory instruments to analyze what they find. Sending research reports to Earth earns mission funding, which players can spend on supplies, new infrastructure, and equipment upgrades that support longer expeditions.

The base runs on interconnected resource and life-support systems. Players extract water from Martian ice and build branching pipe networks on a grid to route resources where they are needed. An electrolyzer uses water and electricity to produce oxygen for the habitat and hydrogen for methane production. Greenhouses grow food using a local water supply, and players can replace crops with genetically modified varieties that grow faster or yield more food. Solar panels, transformers, batteries, and physical power cables let players generate, store, and distribute electricity across the outpost.

The game culminates in a fictional sample-return mission. Players investigate deep ice for a possible sign of microbial life, collect the required geological samples, and use a Sabatier reactor to produce methane for the rocket that sends the samples to Earth.

What makes it creative

Players build the connections between systems themselves and see the consequences of their decisions. If a dust storm reduces solar output and the batteries run down, the electrolyzer can stop, the habitat starts using its oxygen reserves, and the next expedition may have to wait. Scientific research is also part of the survival strategy. A sample collected on one expedition can fund the equipment that makes the next one possible.

Educational benefits and intended impact

Short, age-appropriate descriptions built into the machinery explain how the equipment relates to real aerospace technology. The achievement system guides players through increasingly complex objectives, from collecting their first sample to building a working power grid and preparing the return launch. These tasks introduce In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), the use of local materials such as Martian ice, and Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS), including how an outpost maintains a breathable habitat. We want players to leave the game able to explain why one system depends on another, anticipate a shortage, and adjust their plan. That practice is intended to build critical thinking and spark curiosity about STEM.

Development tools and design choices

We built the game in Godot using GDScript, used GitHub to manage the project, and used AI tools to assist with coding, debugging, and some pixel-art assets. To balance scientific fidelity with a pace suited to ages 7 to 12, we compressed a Martian sol from about 24 hours and 39 minutes to eight minutes, accelerated crop growth, and simplified the electrical grid and industrial processes. Players can therefore experience the day–night cycle, test a change to their base, and observe the result within one session.

The game uses WSA–ENLIL simulations from NASA’s DONKI database to help select the profile of some solar events and represent increases in radiation exposure. The game controls event timing and simulates Martian dust storms separately.
